variants.title: Turn a concern into evidence
variants.context: A bias concern becomes evidence in four steps: declare the harm and the direction that counts as harmful, construct matched cases that hold task meaning constant, sample and score with versioned prompts, decoding, and scorers, then gate on slice intervals and monitor under bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: A stakeholder reports that the assistant treats one group unfairly. Put the measurement work in order.

items.text: Build matched cases with counterfactual substitutions and declare the intersectional slices first.
Compare slice intervals against the threshold and monitor product outcomes under a bounded canary.
Version the model, prompt, decoding policy, automated scorers, and the human-audit rubric, then score.
Name the affected workflow, the metric, the direction of harm, and what crossing the threshold costs.

variants.hint: A complaint is not yet a measurable claim; what turns it into one?
variants.explanation: Declaring the harm and slices before results exist is what stops the threshold from moving after the numbers arrive.

variants.title: Turn a concern into evidence
variants.context: A bias concern becomes evidence in four steps: declare the harm and the direction that counts as harmful, construct matched cases that hold task meaning constant, sample and score with versioned prompts, decoding, and scorers, then gate on slice intervals and monitor under bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: A hiring assistant may refuse disclosure-related questions unevenly. Put the work in order.

items.text: Freeze decoding and the refusal scorer, then collect enough scored samples per slice.
Write matched requests that differ only in the disclosure, and declare the intersectional slices.
Read the gap interval against the declared maximum and watch the same slices after limited exposure.
State that an uneven refusal rate on those questions is the harm and which population it reaches.

variants.hint: The substitution has to be the only thing that changes.
variants.explanation: Controlled comparison means the same task, prompt meaning, sampling policy, and scorer across every group.

variants.title: Turn a concern into evidence
variants.context: A bias concern becomes evidence in four steps: declare the harm and the direction that counts as harmful, construct matched cases that hold task meaning constant, sample and score with versioned prompts, decoding, and scorers, then gate on slice intervals and monitor under bounded exposure.
variants.prompt: A monitoring alert shows a new gap after a model upgrade. Put the response in order.

items.text: Apply the declared gate, then confirm the finding on a held-out suite before changing policy.
Rebuild matched cases against the upgraded system rather than reusing last quarter's generations.
Restate which harm the alert corresponds to and whether that metric was already declared.
Rescore with the versioned scorers and record the new model and prompt revisions.

variants.hint: A newly discovered gap is a hypothesis until it is confirmed somewhere else.
variants.explanation: Discovered failures are confirmed on held-out cases, because many slice tests produce chance discoveries.

variants.title: Operate the fairness loop
variants.context: Fairness runs as a release and monitoring loop: an offline gate blocks clear violations and holds inconclusive slices, shadow and canary expose a bounded cohort, slice monitoring tracks outcomes and scorer drift with minimum-count suppression, and rollback preserves evidence and adds a regression slice before re-release.
variants.prompt: A candidate has just finished offline bias evaluation. Put the deployment loop in order.

items.text: Track outcomes, abstentions, complaints, and scorer drift with privacy-safe slice keys.
Run the candidate on representative traffic, then expose a bounded cohort once the gates pass.
Roll back on the declared thresholds, preserve evidence, and add a regression slice before re-release.
Block clear threshold violations, hold inconclusive slices, and preserve every tested result.

variants.hint: Offline evidence earns exposure; how much?
variants.explanation: A pass earns a canary rather than a global release, because offline evidence cannot cover every production population.

variants.title: Operate the fairness loop
variants.context: Fairness runs as a release and monitoring loop: an offline gate blocks clear violations and holds inconclusive slices, shadow and canary expose a bounded cohort, slice monitoring tracks outcomes and scorer drift with minimum-count suppression, and rollback preserves evidence and adds a regression slice before re-release.
variants.prompt: A canary shows a widening outcome gap for one cohort. Put the response in order.

items.text: Compare the canary cohort against the shadow results collected on the same traffic.
Confirm the gap is not a scorer drift or a denominator collapse in the monitoring keys.
Trigger the declared rollback, keep the affected evidence, and add the cohort as a regression slice.
Check the offline record for whether that slice passed, held, or was never declared.

variants.hint: Before treating it as a model regression, ask whether the measurement moved.
variants.explanation: Monitoring alerts on both outcome gaps and evidence quality, so scorer drift is ruled out before a rollback is attributed.

variants.title: Operate the fairness loop
variants.context: Fairness runs as a release and monitoring loop: an offline gate blocks clear violations and holds inconclusive slices, shadow and canary expose a bounded cohort, slice monitoring tracks outcomes and scorer drift with minimum-count suppression, and rollback preserves evidence and adds a regression slice before re-release.
variants.prompt: A mitigation is proposed after a blocked release. Put the work in order.

items.text: Expose a bounded cohort and monitor task success, refusals, and complaints by slice.
Shadow the mitigated candidate to see how often it intervenes on benign requests.
Rerun the offline gate on the failing slice plus the quality gates the mitigation could disturb.
Keep the rollback threshold armed and record the residual failures that still need human review.

variants.hint: A mitigation changes user-visible behavior, not only the bias metric.
variants.explanation: Mitigations are evaluated on the same traffic contract, since closing a gap can move harm into refusals and lost utility.

variants.title: Size the evaluation
variants.context: Evaluation volume multiplies across the declared dimensions. Slices times prompts per slice times continuations per prompt gives the number of generations, and each automated scorer adds one scoring job per generation. Repeated generations from one prompt stay correlated, so more samples narrow random error without repairing prompt selection.
variants.prompt: A plan declares 8 product-relevant slices, 200 prompts per slice, and 4 continuations per prompt. How many generations does it require?
variants.hint: Multiply the declared dimensions rather than adding them.
variants.explanation: 8 slices times 200 prompts times 4 continuations is 6,400 generations.

mistakes.feedback: That drops the continuations per prompt and counts prompts only.
That adds the three dimensions instead of multiplying them.

variants.title: Size the evaluation
variants.context: Evaluation volume multiplies across the declared dimensions. Slices times prompts per slice times continuations per prompt gives the number of generations, and each automated scorer adds one scoring job per generation. Repeated generations from one prompt stay correlated, so more samples narrow random error without repairing prompt selection.
variants.prompt: A plan declares 10 slices, 150 prompts per slice, and 6 continuations per prompt. How many generations does it require?
variants.hint: Every prompt is drawn more than once, and that factor stays in the product.
variants.explanation: 10 slices times 150 prompts times 6 continuations is 9,000 generations.

mistakes.feedback: That counts prompts and drops the six continuations each one needs.
That adds the dimensions rather than multiplying them.

variants.title: Size the evaluation
variants.context: Evaluation volume multiplies across the declared dimensions. Slices times prompts per slice times continuations per prompt gives the number of generations, and each automated scorer adds one scoring job per generation. Repeated generations from one prompt stay correlated, so more samples narrow random error without repairing prompt selection.
variants.prompt: A plan declares 6 slices, 300 prompts per slice, and 5 continuations per prompt, and every generation is scored by 2 automated scorers. How many scoring jobs does it require?
variants.hint: Work out the generations first, then apply the scorers.
variants.explanation: 6 times 300 times 5 is 9,000 generations, and two scorers each make 18,000 scoring jobs.

mistakes.feedback: That counts generations rather than the scoring jobs they create.
That drops the five continuations per prompt before applying the scorers.

variants.title: Apply the gap gate
variants.context: The gate reads the plausible gap, not the point estimate. When the whole interval sits above the declared maximum the action is block, when the interval crosses the maximum the action is hold for evidence, and when it stays below the maximum the slice is eligible for a bounded canary. A slice under its minimum denominator is held as inconclusive.
variants.prompt: A declared slice shows a harm gap with a 95 percent interval from 7 to 15 points against a declared maximum of 6 points. What is the action?
options: Hold for evidence, because a wider sample could still bring it down.
Release to a canary, because the estimate may drift back toward the limit.
Block, because the entire plausible gap sits above the declared maximum.
optionFeedback: More evidence narrows an interval; it does not move one that already clears the limit.
Exposing users while a confirmed gap stands is exactly what the gate exists to prevent.
When even the lower bound exceeds the maximum, the harm is established rather than uncertain.
variants.hint: Compare the lower bound with the threshold, not the point estimate.
variants.explanation: A lower bound above the maximum names a confirmed harm, so the response is to fix the failing path rather than gather more data.

variants.title: Apply the gap gate
variants.context: The gate reads the plausible gap, not the point estimate. When the whole interval sits above the declared maximum the action is block, when the interval crosses the maximum the action is hold for evidence, and when it stays below the maximum the slice is eligible for a bounded canary. A slice under its minimum denominator is held as inconclusive.
variants.prompt: A declared slice shows a harm gap with a 95 percent interval from minus 1 to 4 points against a declared maximum of 6 points. What is the action?
options: Eligible for a bounded canary, since the plausible gap stays under the maximum.
Block, because the observed gap for that slice is not actually zero.
Hold for evidence, because a negative lower bound means the design failed.
optionFeedback: The whole interval sits below the declared maximum, which is what the passing action requires.
The threshold is a governed tolerance, not a demand that every measured gap be zero.
A negative lower bound simply means the direction is uncertain within the tolerance.
variants.hint: Where does the upper bound sit relative to the maximum?
variants.explanation: A pass earns bounded exposure, because offline evidence supports a canary rather than proving every context is safe.

variants.title: Apply the gap gate
variants.context: The gate reads the plausible gap, not the point estimate. When the whole interval sits above the declared maximum the action is block, when the interval crosses the maximum the action is hold for evidence, and when it stays below the maximum the slice is eligible for a bounded canary. A slice under its minimum denominator is held as inconclusive.
variants.prompt: A declared intersectional slice has 40 scored observations against a minimum denominator of 200, and its interval happens to fall below the maximum. What is the action?
options: Hold for denominator and report the slice as inconclusive in the release table.
Pass the slice, since its measured interval already falls below the maximum.
Drop the slice from the report, because its denominator is too small to read.
optionFeedback: A minimum denominator is required even when a wide interval happens to land under the threshold.
An interval built from 40 observations is too wide to support a pass on this slice.
Dropping declared intersections is how an aggregate hides the most affected people.
variants.hint: The interval is not the only requirement the gate carries.
variants.explanation: Declared intersections stay in the table marked inconclusive, and targeted evidence is collected rather than the slice being dropped.

variants.title: Choose the lens
variants.context: Each method asks a different question. CrowS-Pairs measures paired likelihood preference, BBQ separates unsupported assumptions under ambiguity from accuracy on stated facts, BOLD compares regard distributions across repeated generations, and a product outcome gap measures the deployed stack after retrieval, prompting, moderation, and business rules.
variants.prompt: The question is whether the model names a person from a stereotype when the context never says who did it. Which method tests that?
options: BOLD, comparing regard across many open-ended continuations about each group.
BBQ ambiguous contexts, scoring stereotype answers against appropriate unknown answers.
CrowS-Pairs, comparing likelihoods for a stereotypical and an anti-stereotypical sentence.
optionFeedback: Open-ended regard measures tone in continuations, not an unsupported inference.
Ambiguous contexts are exactly where choosing a person from stereotype is the failure.
Paired likelihood preference is a different behavior and does not involve an unknown answer.
variants.hint: Which method has an unknown answer as the correct response?
variants.explanation: BBQ separates unsupported assumptions under ambiguity from ordinary accuracy on stated facts.

variants.title: Choose the lens
variants.context: Each method asks a different question. CrowS-Pairs measures paired likelihood preference, BBQ separates unsupported assumptions under ambiguity from accuracy on stated facts, BOLD compares regard distributions across repeated generations, and a product outcome gap measures the deployed stack after retrieval, prompting, moderation, and business rules.
variants.prompt: The question is whether one group receives more demeaning language across repeated open-ended continuations. Which method tests that?
options: CrowS-Pairs, comparing the likelihood of two minimally different sentences.
BBQ disambiguated contexts, scoring accuracy on the facts the question states.
BOLD with a frozen sampling policy, comparing full distributions and tail rates.
optionFeedback: A paired likelihood score says nothing about what the model actually generates.
Disambiguated accuracy tests use of stated facts, not the tone of open-ended text.
Rare harmful generations matter, so the comparison uses distributions rather than one completion.
variants.hint: One completion is not enough when decoding is stochastic.
variants.explanation: BOLD compares generation distributions and tails, and repeated generations from one prompt are treated as a cluster.

variants.title: Choose the lens
variants.context: Each method asks a different question. CrowS-Pairs measures paired likelihood preference, BBQ separates unsupported assumptions under ambiguity from accuracy on stated facts, BOLD compares regard distributions across repeated generations, and a product outcome gap measures the deployed stack after retrieval, prompting, moderation, and business rules.
variants.prompt: The question is whether task-success rates differ once retrieval, moderation, and business rules all run. Which method tests that?
options: BOLD regard distributions collected from the model without the product path.
A product outcome measurement on the deployed stack with its own slice keys.
CrowS-Pairs preference rates reported by bias type on the base model.
optionFeedback: Regard measured without the product path leaves out the stages that change the outcome.
Only the deployed path includes the refusal, ranking, and business rules that shape the outcome.
A base-model likelihood score cannot represent what the product finally returns.
variants.hint: Which stages of the system does each method actually exercise?
variants.explanation: Benchmarks probe model behavior, while an outcome gap is measured after prompting, retrieval, moderation, and product rules apply.
